topic.title: Nepal Financial Literacy
topic.shortInfo: Structured money, banking, personal finance, investing, and NEPSE lessons for learners in Nepal.

lessons.title: Why Money Exists
lessons.summary: See why barter fails and why money became necessary.

cards.front: Imagine you have apples but need eggs. What trade problem appears before money exists?
cards.back: Barter: Trading goods directly without money. E.g., 5 apples for 2 eggs. Problem: You need someone who wants exactly what you have!
cards.label: Barter

cards.front: If barter keeps failing, what could everyone agree to accept so trade becomes easier?
cards.back: Money is a medium of exchange — something everyone agrees has value. It solves the barter problem by being accepted by everyone.
cards.label: Medium of Exchange

cards.front: If money is useful every day, what three jobs must it do?
cards.back: The 3 functions of money: 1. Medium of Exchange (buy/sell things) 2. Unit of Account (measure value) 3. Store of Value (save for later)
cards.label: The 3 functions of money

cards.front: Why do people and countries have to make economic choices at all?
cards.back: Scarcity: There isn't enough of everything for everyone. Scarcity is the fundamental reason economics exists.
cards.label: Scarcity

quiz.question: What problem does money solve?
choices: Solves the double coincidence of wants in barter
quiz.explanation: Money solves the barter problem by removing the need for two people to want exactly what the other has at the same time.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a function of money?
quiz.explanation: Money helps people exchange, measure, and store value, but being a source of happiness is not one of its economic functions.

quiz.question: Why does economics exist?
quiz.explanation: Economics exists because resources are limited while human wants keep growing, so choices have to be made.

lessons.title: Nepali Currency: The Rupee
lessons.summary: Understand Nepal's currency, central bank, and exchange rates.

cards.front: What is Nepal's official money called, and who puts it into circulation?
cards.back: Nepali Rupee — Nepal's official currency. Symbol: रू or Rs. Issued by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB).
cards.label: Nepali Rupee

cards.front: Who manages Nepal's money supply and works to keep the rupee stable?
cards.back: Nepal Rastra Bank: Nepal's central bank, established 1956. Controls money supply, sets interest rates, and maintains currency stability.
cards.label: Nepal Rastra Bank

cards.front: If 1 USD equals about 133 NPR, what is that number actually showing?
cards.back: Exchange Rate: How much of one currency you get for another. E.g., 1 USD ≈ 133 NPR. Rates change daily based on trade and market forces.
cards.label: Exchange Rate

cards.front: Why can imports and Nepal's INR link affect how strong the rupee feels?
cards.back: Because Nepal imports more than it exports, trade imbalance weakens NPR. It is also tied closely to the Indian Rupee (INR).
cards.label: What affects NPR

quiz.question: Which institution issues Nepali currency?
quiz.explanation: Nepal Rastra Bank is the central bank that issues and manages the Nepali rupee.

quiz.question: Nepal's currency is pegged closely to:
quiz.explanation: The Nepali rupee is closely linked to the Indian rupee, which strongly influences its exchange relationship.

quiz.question: Exchange rate means:
choices: How much one currency buys of another
quiz.explanation: An exchange rate tells you how much of one currency can be traded for another currency.

lessons.title: Inflation: Why Things Get Expensive
lessons.summary: Learn why prices rise and how inflation affects daily life.

cards.front: If momo cost more this year than last year, what economic idea are you seeing in action?
cards.back: Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. If momo cost Rs.50 last year and Rs.60 now — that's 20% inflation on momos!
cards.label: Inflation

cards.front: When prices rise across the economy, what forces can be driving it?
cards.back: Causes of inflation: 1. Too much money chasing too few goods 2. Supply disruptions (less goods) 3. Demand surge (more buyers) 4. Import costs rising
cards.label: Causes of inflation

cards.front: How do economists track whether everyday goods are getting more expensive?
cards.back: CPI (Consumer Price Index) measures inflation by tracking prices of a 'basket' of everyday goods like rice, oil, vegetables, and transport.
cards.label: CPI

cards.front: If your savings stay the same but prices keep rising, what happens to your buying power?
cards.back: Your Rs.1,000 buys less every year. Savings lose purchasing power. Fixed-income earners suffer most.
cards.label: Purchasing Power

cards.front: Is all inflation bad, or does the level of inflation change the story?
cards.back: Mild inflation (2-4%) = healthy economy. High inflation (10%+) = economic stress. Deflation (negative) = also bad — people stop spending.
cards.label: Inflation Levels

quiz.question: If your salary stays at Rs.50,000 but inflation is 10%, what happens?
quiz.explanation: When prices rise but your salary stays the same, your money buys fewer goods and services than before.

quiz.question: What does CPI measure?
choices: Changes in prices of everyday goods
quiz.explanation: CPI tracks the changing prices of a basket of common goods and services to estimate inflation.

quiz.question: What is 'hyperinflation'?
quiz.explanation: Hyperinflation is an extreme and rapid rise in prices that destroys normal purchasing power.

lessons.title: How Banks Work
lessons.summary: See how banks use deposits, loans, and reserves to operate.

cards.front: If banks take deposits and give loans, where does their profit actually come from?
cards.back: Banks take deposits from savers and lend that money to borrowers. They charge borrowers more interest than they pay savers — that's their profit.
cards.label: Bank Profit Model

cards.front: If you deposit Rs.100, why does the bank keep only part of it in cash?
cards.back: Fractional Reserve Banking: Banks only keep a fraction of deposits in cash. The rest is loaned out. If you deposit Rs.100, the bank might lend Rs.90 and keep Rs.10.
cards.label: Fractional Reserve Banking

cards.front: What happens if too many depositors try to withdraw at the same time?
cards.back: Bank Run: When everyone tries to withdraw their money at once. Banks can't fulfill this because money is lent out. This caused collapses in the Great Depression.
cards.label: Bank Run

cards.front: What main kinds of banking institutions operate in Nepal?
cards.back: Types of banks in Nepal: 1. Commercial Banks (e.g., NIC Asia, Nabil) 2. Development Banks 3. Finance Companies 4. Microfinance Institutions 5. Nepal Rastra Bank (central bank)
cards.label: Types of banks in Nepal

quiz.question: How do banks make profit?
choices: Charging higher interest to borrowers than they pay savers
quiz.explanation: Banks earn money mainly from the gap between the interest they charge borrowers and the interest they pay savers.

quiz.question: What is fractional reserve banking?
choices: Banks lend out most deposits, keeping only a fraction
quiz.explanation: In fractional reserve banking, a bank keeps only part of deposits as cash and lends the rest out.

quiz.question: Nepal's central bank is:
quiz.explanation: Nepal Rastra Bank is the central bank responsible for monetary policy and financial regulation.

lessons.title: Savings vs Fixed Deposits
lessons.summary: Compare savings accounts and fixed deposits based on your goals.

cards.front: If you need flexible access to money, what kind of account fits best?
cards.back: Savings Account: Flexible account. Withdraw anytime. Low interest (2-4% in Nepal). Good for emergency funds and daily expenses.
cards.label: Savings Account

cards.front: If you can lock money away for longer, what bank product usually pays more?
cards.back: Fixed Deposit (FD): Lock money for fixed period (3 months to 5 years). Higher interest (7-11% in Nepal). Penalty if withdrawn early.
cards.label: Fixed Deposit (FD)

cards.front: If you need cash soon versus later, how would you choose between savings and an FD?
cards.back: Which to choose depends on goal: Need money soon → Savings Account. Won't need money for 1+ year → Fixed Deposit. Best strategy: Keep 3 months expenses in savings, rest in FD.
cards.label: Which to choose depends on goal

cards.front: If your deposit earns interest but prices also rise, how do you know your real gain?
cards.back: Real Return = Interest Rate - Inflation Rate. If FD gives 8% but inflation is 7%, your real return is just 1%. You barely grew your money!
cards.label: Real Return

quiz.question: Which gives higher interest in Nepal?
quiz.explanation: Fixed deposits usually offer higher interest because the money stays locked in for a fixed period.

quiz.question: If inflation is 8% and your FD rate is 9%, your real return is:
quiz.explanation: Real return is calculated after inflation, so 9% interest minus 8% inflation leaves only a 1% gain in buying power.

quiz.question: Emergency fund should ideally be in:
quiz.explanation: Emergency money should stay liquid and easy to access, so a savings or other liquid account is safer than locked or risky assets.

lessons.title: Loans, EMI & Interest
lessons.summary: Understand EMI, interest, and how to judge good versus bad debt.

cards.front: When you repay a loan every month, what exactly is an EMI?
cards.back: EMI (Equated Monthly Installment): Fixed amount paid every month to repay a loan. Includes both principal and interest.
cards.label: EMI (Equated Monthly Installment)

cards.front: Why does compound interest grow much faster than simple interest over time?
cards.back: Simple Interest: Interest only on principal. Compound Interest: Interest on principal + previous interest. Compound grows MUCH faster. Good for investing, bad for loans.
cards.label: Simple Interest

cards.front: How can you tell the difference between useful debt and harmful debt?
cards.back: Good Debt: Builds wealth (education loan, home loan). Bad Debt: Loses value (loan for gadgets, luxury). Worst Debt: High-interest consumer loans (30%+ APR).
cards.label: Good Debt

cards.front: Why does your credit history matter before a bank decides your next loan?
cards.back: CIB (Credit Information Bureau) tracks your loan repayment history. Good score = lower interest rates on future loans. Bad score = harder to borrow.
cards.label: Credit History

quiz.question: What makes compound interest powerful?
quiz.explanation: Compound interest is powerful because interest is earned not only on the original amount but also on earlier interest.

quiz.question: Which is considered 'bad debt'?
quiz.explanation: A luxury phone loan usually finances consumption, not an asset that grows income or long-term value.

quiz.question: CIB in Nepal tracks:
quiz.explanation: CIB records your loan repayment history, which lenders use to judge your credit reliability.

lessons.title: Income, Expenses & Budget
lessons.summary: Build a simple budget using income, expenses, and allocation rules.

cards.front: After taxes are deducted from salary, what amount actually reaches you?
cards.back: Net Income: Your take-home pay AFTER taxes. If salary is Rs.60,000 and tax is Rs.5,000, net income = Rs.55,000.
cards.label: Net Income

cards.front: If you budget one month's income, how does the 50/30/20 rule divide it?
cards.back: 50/30/20 Rule: 50% → Needs (rent, food, transport). 30% → Wants (eating out, Netflix). 20% → Savings & debt repayment.
cards.label: 50/30/20 Rule

cards.front: Which expenses stay steady each month, and which ones can move around?
cards.back: Fixed expenses: Same every month (rent, loan EMI). Variable expenses: Changes monthly (groceries, entertainment). Control variable expenses to save more.
cards.label: Fixed expenses

cards.front: What does it mean to give every rupee a job before the month starts?
cards.back: Zero-based budgeting: Assign every rupee a job. Income - All Expenses = 0. Every rupee is allocated to SOMETHING (including savings).
cards.label: Zero-based budgeting

quiz.question: In the 50/30/20 rule, 20% goes to:
quiz.explanation: In this rule, the last 20% is meant for saving money and reducing debt.

quiz.question: Which is a FIXED expense?
quiz.explanation: Rent is usually a fixed expense because the amount normally stays the same from month to month.

quiz.question: Net income is:
quiz.explanation: Net income is the amount you actually take home after tax and other deductions are removed.

lessons.title: Emergency Fund: Your Safety Net
lessons.summary: Create a cash buffer for shocks before they become debt problems.

cards.front: What kind of money should be used for a medical shock or sudden job loss?
cards.back: An emergency fund is money saved specifically for unexpected events: job loss, medical emergency, urgent repair. NOT for sales, trips, or impulse buys.
cards.label: Emergency Fund

cards.front: How big should an emergency fund be if you want a real safety buffer?
cards.back: Target: 3-6 months of your monthly expenses. If you spend Rs.30,000/month, target Rs.90,000–1,80,000 in emergency fund.
cards.label: Target

cards.front: Where should emergency money stay so it is both safe and quickly accessible?
cards.back: Keep it in: High-interest savings account or liquid mutual fund. NOT in stocks (can crash when you need it most). Must be accessible within 1-2 days.
cards.label: Keep it in

cards.front: Why is an emergency fund especially important for many households in Nepal?
cards.back: Nepal reality: Most Nepalis can't cover a Rs.10,000 emergency without borrowing. Remittance-dependent families are especially vulnerable if the main earner falls ill.
cards.label: Nepal reality

quiz.question: Emergency fund should cover how many months of expenses?
quiz.explanation: A 3 to 6 month cushion is a common safety target because it can cover many short-term emergencies or income shocks.

quiz.question: Where should you NOT keep your emergency fund?
quiz.explanation: The stock market is too volatile for emergency savings because prices can fall right when you need cash.

quiz.question: Emergency fund is for:
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund is meant for real financial shocks like illness, repairs, or job loss, not optional spending.

lessons.title: FOMO, Lifestyle Inflation & Traps
lessons.summary: Spot the behavior traps that quietly destroy savings.

cards.front: When you see other people spending online, what emotional trap can push you to overspend?
cards.back: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out): Seeing friends buy iPhones, go to Maldives, drive new cars — and feeling pressure to match them. Leads to overspending and debt.
cards.label: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out)

cards.front: Why do some people earn more but still never feel ahead?
cards.back: Lifestyle Inflation: When income rises, expenses rise to match it. Earned Rs.10,000 more? Suddenly 'need' a better phone, fancier food, pricier rent. Net savings = same as before.
cards.label: Lifestyle Inflation

cards.front: Why is comparing your life to social media often financially dangerous?
cards.back: The Comparison Trap: Social media shows you the highlight reel. That friend in Maldives might have credit card debt. That new car might be on a 7-year loan. Compare outcomes, not appearances.
cards.label: The Comparison Trap

cards.front: Why can past spending trick you into continuing a bad decision?
cards.back: Sunk Cost Fallacy: Continuing something bad because you already invested in it. 'I paid Rs.5,000 for this course so I must finish it.' The Rs.5,000 is gone either way — make the best decision NOW.
cards.label: Sunk Cost Fallacy

quiz.question: Lifestyle inflation means:
choices: Expenses growing as fast as income, with no net savings gain
quiz.explanation: Lifestyle inflation happens when your spending rises with your income, leaving little or no extra savings.

quiz.question: The sunk cost fallacy is:
choices: Continuing a bad decision because of past investment
quiz.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing a bad decision just because you have already spent money, time, or effort on it.

quiz.question: To avoid FOMO-spending, you should:
choices: Compare your financial progress to your own past self
quiz.explanation: Comparing yourself to your own goals and progress helps reduce pressure to copy other people's spending.

lessons.title: What is the Share Market?
lessons.summary: Understand shares, NEPSE, and why companies list on the market.

cards.front: If you buy shares of Nabil Bank, what do you actually own?
cards.back: A share is a small ownership piece of a company. If Nabil Bank has 1 crore shares and you own 100, you own 0.0001% of Nabil Bank and share in its profits.
cards.label: Share Ownership

cards.front: Where are listed shares actually bought and sold in Nepal?
cards.back: NEPSE: Nepal Stock Exchange. Nepal's only stock exchange where shares are bought and sold. Located in Kathmandu, established in 1993.
cards.label: NEPSE

cards.front: Why would a company raise money from the public instead of taking only loans?
cards.back: Why companies list: To raise capital (money) from the public without taking loans. You give them money; they give you ownership shares. Win-win if the company grows.
cards.label: Why companies list

cards.front: What do bull and bear markets tell you about prices and investor mood?
cards.back: Bull Market: Prices rising, optimism, everyone buying. Bear Market: Prices falling, fear, everyone selling. NEPSE has experienced both dramatically — 2020-21 was a major bull run.
cards.label: Bull Market

quiz.question: NEPSE stands for:
quiz.explanation: NEPSE is short for Nepal Stock Exchange, the main market where listed shares are traded in Nepal.

quiz.question: If you buy 10 shares of a company, you become:
quiz.explanation: Buying shares makes you a part owner of the company, even if your ownership is very small.

quiz.question: A bear market means:
quiz.explanation: A bear market describes a period when prices are generally falling and investor sentiment is negative.

lessons.title: IPO: Getting In Early
lessons.summary: Learn how IPOs work in Nepal from application to listing day.

cards.front: What is happening when a company offers shares to the public for the first time?
cards.back: IPO (Initial Public Offering): The FIRST time a company sells shares to the public. Nepal's IPO culture is massive — people apply hoping for allotment and quick profit.
cards.label: IPO (Initial Public Offering)

cards.front: If an IPO opens today, what steps would you follow to apply properly in Nepal?
cards.back: How to apply for IPO in Nepal: 1. Open DEMAT account (Mero Share) 2. Link bank account 3. Apply via Mero Share app during open window 4. Pay application amount 5. Wait for allotment lottery.
cards.label: How to apply for IPO in Nepal

cards.front: What account do you need in Nepal to hold shares electronically?
cards.back: DEMAT Account: Dematerialized account — stores your shares electronically. Like a bank account but for stocks. Required to trade on NEPSE. Opened through brokers or banks.
cards.label: DEMAT Account

cards.front: If an IPO is heavily oversubscribed in Nepal, does applying for more units improve your odds?
cards.back: In Nepal, IPOs are massively oversubscribed (10x-100x demand). So it's a lottery. Applying for more units doesn't help — it's 1 unit per application.
cards.label: Oversubscription

cards.front: After IPO shares are allotted and start trading, what can happen to the price?
cards.back: After allotment, shares start trading on NEPSE secondary market. Price can go up (profit) or down (loss) from issue price. Many Nepali IPOs list above issue price — but not always.
cards.label: Secondary Market

quiz.question: What is Mero Share used for in Nepal?
choices: Applying for IPOs and managing shares
quiz.explanation: Mero Share is used to apply for IPOs and to view or manage your share holdings electronically.

quiz.question: In Nepal's oversubscribed IPO, applying for more units:
choices: Doesn't increase chances — it's 1 application per person
quiz.explanation: In heavily oversubscribed Nepalese IPOs, applying for more units does not improve the basic allotment chance per applicant.

quiz.question: DEMAT account is:
choices: An electronic account holding your shares
quiz.explanation: A DEMAT account stores your shares electronically, similar to how a bank account stores money.

lessons.title: Reading Share Prices & Indicators
lessons.summary: Decode the core numbers investors use to read NEPSE stocks.

cards.front: When the NEPSE index rises or falls, what bigger market story is it telling?
cards.back: NEPSE Index: A number representing the overall value of all NEPSE-listed shares. If NEPSE index rises from 2000 to 2200, the market overall gained 10%.
cards.label: NEPSE Index

cards.front: How do you estimate the total market value of a listed company?
cards.back: Market Capitalization: Total value of a company = Share Price × Total Shares. E.g., if Nabil Bank has 10 crore shares at Rs.1000 each, market cap = Rs.10 arba.
cards.label: Market Capitalization

cards.front: If investors talk about P/E, what are they comparing?
cards.back: P/E Ratio (Price-to-Earnings): How much you pay per rupee of profit. P/E = Share Price ÷ Earnings Per Share. Lower P/E = potentially cheaper. High P/E = market expects high growth.
cards.label: P/E Ratio (Price-to-Earnings)

cards.front: If a company earns profit, how do you translate that into earnings per share?
cards.back: EPS (Earnings Per Share): Company's annual profit ÷ number of shares. EPS of Rs.50 means the company earned Rs.50 per share this year.
cards.label: EPS (Earnings Per Share)

cards.front: How does a company return part of its profit to shareholders?
cards.back: Dividend: A portion of company profit given to shareholders. Nepal banks often give 10-25% dividends. Types: Cash dividend (actual money) or Stock dividend (extra shares).
cards.label: Dividend

quiz.question: If NEPSE index falls from 2500 to 2000, the market:
quiz.explanation: A fall of 500 points from 2500 is a 20% drop, so the market has fallen by one-fifth.

quiz.question: P/E ratio of 15 means:
choices: You're paying Rs.15 for every Rs.1 of company earnings
quiz.explanation: A P/E of 15 means investors are paying Rs.15 in share price for every Rs.1 of the company's earnings.

quiz.question: A cash dividend means:
choices: Company pays you actual money per share
quiz.explanation: A cash dividend means the company distributes actual money to shareholders for each share they own.

lessons.title: Types of Companies on NEPSE
lessons.summary: Recognize the major sectors that make up Nepal's stock market.

cards.front: If someone mentions the banking sector on NEPSE, what type of companies should you picture?
cards.back: Banking Sector: Largest sector on NEPSE. Commercial banks like Nabil, NIC Asia, Standard Chartered. Generally stable with regular dividends. Regulated by NRB.
cards.label: Banking Sector

cards.front: What makes hydropower companies an important Nepal-specific sector on NEPSE?
cards.back: Hydropower Sector: Nepal's growing sector. Companies like Upper Tamakoshi, NHPC. Long construction phase, then stable revenue. Connected to Nepal's energy future.
cards.label: Hydropower Sector

cards.front: Which companies belong to the insurance sector, and who regulates them?
cards.back: Insurance Sector: Life and non-life insurance companies. Life insurance: Nepal Life, NLGI. Regulated by Insurance Board (Beema Samiti).
cards.label: Insurance Sector

cards.front: How is the finance sector different from the biggest banking names on NEPSE?
cards.back: Finance Sector: Development banks and finance companies. Higher risk, potentially higher return. Microfinance serves rural Nepal — some listed on NEPSE.
cards.label: Finance Sector

cards.front: Which real-economy businesses fall under the manufacturing sector?
cards.back: Manufacturing Sector: Companies like Bottlers Nepal (Coca-Cola), Unilever Nepal. Smaller sector on NEPSE but growing.
cards.label: Manufacturing Sector

quiz.question: Which sector dominates NEPSE by market cap?
quiz.explanation: Banking has historically been one of the largest and most influential sectors in the Nepali market.

quiz.question: Hydropower companies in Nepal primarily generate revenue from:
quiz.explanation: Hydropower firms earn by producing electricity and selling that power into the energy system.

quiz.question: Insurance companies in Nepal are regulated by:
quiz.explanation: Insurance companies are overseen by the Insurance Board, also known as Beema Samiti.

lessons.title: Risk & Return
lessons.summary: Learn why every return comes with risk and how to manage that trade-off.

cards.front: What trade-off do investors accept when they chase higher returns?
cards.back: Risk-Return Relationship: Higher potential return = higher risk. FD: Low risk, low return. Stocks: High risk, high potential return. No free lunch in investing.
cards.label: Risk-Return Relationship

cards.front: What different kinds of risk can hurt an investment even if the idea looked good?
cards.back: Types of risk: Market risk (overall market falls), Company risk (specific company fails), Liquidity risk (can't sell when you want), Inflation risk (returns don't beat inflation).
cards.label: Types of risk

cards.front: How do you reduce damage when one investment goes wrong?
cards.back: Diversification: Don't put all eggs in one basket. Spread across sectors (banking + hydro + insurance) and asset types (stocks + FD + gold). If one falls, others cushion the blow.
cards.label: Diversification

cards.front: Why does the amount of time you can stay invested change how much risk you can take?
cards.back: Time Horizon: How long you can leave money invested. Short term (under 3 years): Low risk instruments. Long term (10+ years): Can afford more volatility for higher returns.
cards.label: Time Horizon

quiz.question: Which has the LOWEST risk?
quiz.explanation: Fixed deposits are generally lower risk than stocks or crypto because returns are more predictable and capital is more protected.

quiz.question: Diversification helps by:
quiz.explanation: Diversification reduces damage from any single investment going wrong by spreading risk across different assets.

quiz.question: For a 20-year investment goal, you should:
choices: Accept more volatility for higher returns
quiz.explanation: A long time horizon allows investors to tolerate more short-term volatility in pursuit of stronger long-term returns.

lessons.title: Mutual Funds in Nepal
lessons.summary: See how mutual funds help small investors diversify in Nepal.

cards.front: If you cannot pick stocks yourself, what structure lets many investors pool money together?
cards.back: A mutual fund is a pool of money from many investors, managed by a professional fund manager. They invest in stocks, bonds, etc. You get units representing your share.
cards.label: Mutual Fund

cards.front: If you want diversification without picking every stock yourself, what mutual fund options exist in Nepal?
cards.back: Nepal's mutual funds: NEPSE has listed mutual funds. Examples: Nabil Equity Fund, Laxmi Value Fund, NMB Saral Bachat. Minimum investment often as low as Rs.1,000.
cards.label: Nepal's mutual funds

cards.front: When a mutual fund quotes its NAV, what number are you really looking at?
cards.back: NAV (Net Asset Value): Price per unit of a mutual fund. If NAV is Rs.12 and you invest Rs.12,000, you get 1,000 units. NAV changes daily based on fund's portfolio.
cards.label: NAV (Net Asset Value)

cards.front: If two funds invest differently, how does active management compare with simply tracking an index?
cards.back: Active vs Passive: Active funds — manager picks stocks, trying to beat market, higher fees. Passive funds — tracks an index (like NEPSE index), lower fees. Research shows passive often outperforms active long-term.
cards.label: Active vs Passive

quiz.question: NAV stands for:
quiz.explanation: NAV means Net Asset Value, which is the per-unit value of a mutual fund after accounting for its holdings.

quiz.question: Which typically has lower management fees?
quiz.explanation: Passive index funds usually charge less because they track an index instead of paying managers to actively pick investments.

quiz.question: A mutual fund allows small investors to:
choices: Access diversified portfolio with less capital
quiz.explanation: Mutual funds let smaller investors access a diversified portfolio without needing enough money to buy every asset individually.

lessons.title: Warren Buffett's Rules
lessons.summary: Use Buffett's core principles to think more clearly about investing.

cards.front: What investing rule matters most if you want to survive long enough to compound?
cards.back: Rule #1: Never Lose Money. Rule #2: Never forget Rule #1. Protecting capital matters more than chasing gains. Losing 50% requires 100% gain just to recover.
cards.label: Rule #1

cards.front: Why should you avoid investing in businesses you do not understand?
cards.back: Buy What You Understand: Only invest in businesses you understand. Buffett avoided tech stocks for decades because he didn't understand their moat. He understood Coca-Cola — simple, consistent, global.
cards.label: Buy What You Understand

cards.front: What changes when you hold a great company for years instead of trading it constantly?
cards.back: Long-Term Thinking: 'Our favorite holding period is forever.' Great companies compound over decades. Short-term trading is expensive (taxes, fees) and emotionally exhausting.
cards.label: Long-Term Thinking

cards.front: How should you react when the market becomes euphoric or fearful?
cards.back: Mr. Market: Benjamin Graham's idea — imagine Mr. Market comes daily offering to buy or sell. He's sometimes euphoric (overpriced) and sometimes depressed (underpriced). Your job: Don't follow his mood. Buy when he's scared.
cards.label: Mr. Market

cards.front: Why is it safer to invest inside your own circle of competence?
cards.back: Circle of Competence: Know what you know. Know what you don't know. Only invest in areas within your competence. Expand the circle slowly but never pretend it's bigger than it is.
cards.label: Circle of Competence

quiz.question: Buffett's most important investing rule is:
quiz.explanation: Buffett emphasizes protecting capital first, because large losses are very hard to recover from.

quiz.question: Mr. Market is depressed and selling shares cheaply. You should:
choices: Consider buying — it's a potential opportunity
quiz.explanation: If prices are low for emotional reasons rather than business weakness, that can create a buying opportunity.

quiz.question: Buffett prefers to hold great companies:
quiz.explanation: Buffett favors long holding periods so strong businesses can compound value over many years.

lessons.title: Technical Analysis Basics
lessons.summary: Read the main chart signals traders watch in the market.

cards.front: What are traders trying to learn when they study charts and patterns?
cards.back: Technical Analysis: Studying past price charts and patterns to predict future price movements. Based on the idea that price patterns repeat. Used by traders (not long-term investors).
cards.label: Technical Analysis

cards.front: When traders talk about support and resistance, what price behavior are they watching?
cards.back: Support & Resistance: Support = price level where stock tends to stop falling (buyers step in). Resistance = price level where stock tends to stop rising (sellers step in). Breaking these levels is significant.
cards.label: Support & Resistance

cards.front: What does a moving average help you see on a price chart?
cards.back: Moving Averages: Average price over a period (50-day MA, 200-day MA). If short-term MA crosses above long-term MA = 'Golden Cross' (bullish). Opposite = 'Death Cross' (bearish).
cards.label: Moving Averages

cards.front: Why does heavy or light trading volume matter when a stock moves?
cards.back: Volume: Number of shares traded. High volume on price rise = strong move. High volume on price fall = panic selling. Low volume moves are less reliable.
cards.label: Volume

cards.front: What does RSI try to tell you about whether a stock is overbought or oversold?
cards.back: RSI (Relative Strength Index): Measures if stock is overbought or oversold. RSI above 70 = overbought (may fall). RSI below 30 = oversold (may rise). Range: 0-100.
cards.label: RSI (Relative Strength Index)

quiz.question: Support level is where:
quiz.explanation: Support is the price zone where buying interest often becomes strong enough to slow or stop a decline.

quiz.question: A Golden Cross occurs when:
choices: Short-term MA crosses above long-term MA
quiz.explanation: A Golden Cross happens when a shorter moving average rises above a longer one, often seen as a bullish signal.

quiz.question: RSI below 30 suggests the stock is:
quiz.explanation: An RSI below 30 usually signals the stock may be oversold after heavy selling pressure.

lessons.title: Fundamental Analysis for NEPSE
lessons.summary: Check business quality and valuation before buying a stock.

cards.front: If you ignore the chart for a moment, what business facts should you study instead?
cards.back: Fundamental Analysis: Evaluating a company's actual business health — revenues, profits, debt, management quality. Used to find undervalued stocks to buy and hold.
cards.label: Fundamental Analysis

cards.front: Which banking ratios should you check before trusting a Nepali bank's fundamentals?
cards.back: Key ratios for Nepal banks: NPA (Non-Performing Assets %) — lower is better. CDR (Credit to Deposit Ratio) — NRB mandates under 90%. ROE (Return on Equity) — how efficiently using shareholder money.
cards.label: Key ratios for Nepal banks

cards.front: If a stock trades below its book value, what might that signal?
cards.back: Book Value per Share: Company's net assets ÷ shares. If BV = Rs.200 and share price = Rs.150, it's trading BELOW book value — potentially undervalued. Price-to-Book ratio < 1 often seen as cheap.
cards.label: Book Value per Share

cards.front: If you open an annual report, which sections deserve the most attention first?
cards.back: Reading Annual Reports: Key sections — Chairman's message (vision), Financial statements (profit/loss), Notes to accounts (hidden details), Auditor's report (red flags). Available on NEPSE website.
cards.label: Reading Annual Reports

quiz.question: High NPA ratio in a bank means:
choices: More loans going bad — bad sign
quiz.explanation: A high NPA ratio means more loans are not being repaid properly, which is a warning sign for the bank.

quiz.question: If Price-to-Book ratio is below 1, the stock:
choices: May be trading below its asset value
quiz.explanation: A price-to-book ratio below 1 can suggest the market values the company below its net asset base.

quiz.question: Annual reports in Nepal are available on:
quiz.explanation: Listed company reports are commonly published through NEPSE and related official disclosures.

lessons.title: Rights Shares & Bonus Shares
lessons.summary: Understand how common corporate actions change your holdings.

cards.front: What right do existing shareholders get in a rights issue?
cards.back: Rights Shares: Existing shareholders get the 'right' to buy new shares at a discounted price. E.g., 1:10 rights means for every 10 shares you own, you can buy 1 new share at Rs.100 (vs market price of Rs.500).
cards.label: Rights Shares

cards.front: What happens when a company gives shareholders bonus shares from reserves?
cards.back: Bonus Shares: Free shares given from company's reserves. 20% bonus = for every 100 shares, you get 20 more free. Share price adjusts down proportionally — but you have more shares.
cards.label: Bonus Shares

cards.front: If a company gives bonus shares, are you instantly richer or does the price adjust?
cards.back: Is bonus really free money? Not exactly. If 20% bonus, share price drops ~20% on ex-date. Your total value stays roughly same. But long-term, if company keeps earning well, more shares = more dividends later.
cards.label: Bonus Share Reality

cards.front: What date decides whether you qualify for a dividend or bonus share?
cards.back: Book Closure Date: Date when company records who owns shares for dividends/bonuses. Own shares BEFORE this date to qualify. After this, price drops by roughly dividend amount (ex-dividend date).
cards.label: Book Closure Date

quiz.question: A 1:5 rights share offer means:
choices: You get 1 free share for every 5 owned
For every 5 shares, you can BUY 1 new at discounted price
quiz.explanation: A 1:5 rights issue means an existing shareholder can buy 1 new share for every 5 shares already owned.

quiz.question: After 20% bonus share, the share price typically:
quiz.explanation: Bonus shares increase the number of shares outstanding, so the market price usually adjusts downward proportionally.

quiz.question: You must own shares BEFORE which date to receive dividend?
quiz.explanation: You need to hold the shares before the book closure date so your name is recorded as eligible for the dividend.
